Garbage, also known as trash, rubbish, or refuse, is waste discarded by humans, usually because it is no longer considered valuable or usable. The term generally excludes metabolic waste, liquid or gaseous wastes, or toxic waste. Garbage is commonly categorized as municipal solid waste.

Throughout its history, garbage has taken various forms, and treatment methods have had varying impacts on the environment. The increase in environmental pollution caused by garbage has resulted in regulation and civic organization efforts.

Garbage management includes waste prevention, reuse, recycling, composting and disposal through landfilling or incineration. Waste-management hierarchies generally prioritize prevention and recovery over disposal.
The mismanagement of human garbage has resulted in numerous ongoing environmental disasters, most notably microplastic contamination, urban litter, and the highly visible Great Pacific Garbage Patch.
Terminology

The word garbage (possibly from Anglo-Norman) originally referred to chicken giblets and other entrails, as recorded in the 15th-century English manuscript A Boke of Kokery, which contains a recipe for Garbage.

In modern usage, the terms garbage, trash, refuse, rubbish and waste are often used interchangeably in different regions, although some terms historically had more specific meanings. Those related terms also have distinct origins reflecting different types of discarded material.

Trash, likely of Scandinavian origin (compare Old Norse tros, meaning "fallen leaves and twigs"), originally denoted woody yard debris and brushwood but was being used to refer to domestic waste in North American English by the early 20th century.

Rubbish derives from late Middle English from the Anglo-Norman rubbous, and may be related to Old French robe ('spoils'), it may be compared with rubble. Refuse entered English from the Old French refuser ('to reject') and has been used since the Late Middle Ages as a formal term for rejected or worthless items.
Waste, related to Latin vastus ('unoccupied' or 'uncultivated'), initially described barren land before the meaning expanded to encompass unused, surplus, or discarded materials.

What constitutes garbage is naturally subjective, as materials discarded by a person or society may be considered useful or capable of restoration by another, hinting to the well known phrase "one man's trash is another man's treasure". Garbage discarded outside designated collection or disposal systems, like trash cans, is generally considered litter.
Unlike waste handled through established waste management systems, litter is improperly deposited in the environment.

In the United States during the 1880s, discarded materials were commonly divided into four categories: ashes, garbage, rubbish and street sweepings. Garbage referred primarily to decomposable organic matter, including kitchen and food scraps, while rubbish encompassed dry materials such as paper, glass, metal, wood, and textiles.

Food waste was sometimes fed to livestock, processed to recover fats and oils, or converted into fertilizer, while rubbish could be recovered and reused in manufacturing. Some of these distinctions remain today, and a more general term is "municipal solid waste".

The distinction between wet and dry waste influenced early municipal collection and disposal practices. Separating organic waste remains important in modern waste management, particularly for recycling and biological treatment.
In the European Union, the Waste Framework Directive required member states to ensure that bio-waste is separated and recycled at source or collected separately subject to specific exceptions.
History
Prehistoric and ancient times

For much of human history, garbage has been a part of daily life. Some of the earliest archaeological evidence of garbage disposal includes pits of oyster shells and animal bones left over from communal eating practices, as well as stone fragments discarded from toolmaking.

The degree to which groups of early humans engaged in agriculture can be estimated by examining the type and quality of animal bones in their garbage. Garbage from prehistoric or pre-civilization humans was collected into mounds called middens, which might contain things such as "a mix of discarded food, charcoal, shell tools, and broken pottery".
In the Neolithic city of Çatalhöyük, garbage was disposed of between homes. Over time, it became a layer that fused buildings together, and later a sublayer upon which other houses were constructed.

In ancient Mesopotamia, cities grew larger and waste management systems began to emerge. Both Abu Salabikh and Tell Brak had designated areas for garbage disposal. Garbage piles were usually seen as places to be avoided, but there is no clear evidence that garbage was understood to be a vector for diseases.

The Indus Valley Civilization had one of the earliest known systems for dealing with wastewater and garbage. The city of Mohenjo-daro had an advanced system for removing sewage. In some parts of the city, every house had a bathroom.
Wastewater flowed from the houses into the street drains, and some of it ran into pits at street level. Some houses used clay (terracotta) pipes to carry waste along the street.

The drains, cesspits, and soak pits had to be kept clear for continued use and were thought to have needed regular cleaning by a large team of workers. Similar drainage systems have been found at other Harappan cities and towns, including Harappa, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, Lothal, and Kalibangan. Not all waste went into drains and pits.

Some abandoned buildings are known to be filled with garbage over time. At Harappa, people living nearby used the streets as dumping areas, so it has been suggested that wooden carts took garbage away from the streets and storage pits, and that the streets were swept regularly.

Smaller rural settlements seem to have used simpler methods. For example, in the village of Farmana garbage pits held broken pottery and possibly food waste, and ash, bones and leftover craft material were dumped on the streets.

In the Minoan civilization, solid waste in the capital of Knossos was put into large pits, covered at intervals with layers of earth. 6 km) from the city to reduce disease spread and keep the city clean.
The city also removed waste outside city boundaries when it came under imminent attack to prevent attackers from scaling over city walls using the garbage piles.

In Ancient Rome, sophisticated aqueducts and other systems for waste removal were built, vast groups of sewers were built, and became known as the Cloaca Maxima. They emptied into the Tiber river, resulting in a large concentration of pollution. There were different qualities of waste management practices depending on one's social standing.

Due to the abundant usage of amphora, an artificial mound, the Monte Testaccio, was formed composing almost entirely of discarded amphora. Access to plumbing as well as sewers was considered a status in Roman culture. Compared to Mesopotamia, Roman waste management was more sophisticated and also more dependent on one's socioeconomic status.

In ancient China, successive dynasties regulated urban refuse through legal penalties and state-organized collection. During the Tang dynasty, authorities punished public littering with caning, while private entrepreneurs profited by collecting urban waste and human excreta to sell to farmers as fertilizer.
By the Song dynasty, the government established dedicated street-cleaning agencies employing hundreds of official scavengers to maintain urban sanitation.
Middle Ages

The Olmec civilization had a systemic way of managing waste. They deposited household garbage into trash-filled pits, open-air middens, and managed water using stone aqueducts. The Olmecs relied on biodegradable materials such as wood, woven fibers, and gourds for everyday use.

Because of this, their primarily organic waste decayed rapidly in the humid climate of the Gulf Coast of Mexico. Olmec garbage deposits filled with layers of broken pottery helped archaeologists Michael Coe and Richard Diehl establish the first chronological timeline of Olmec history.

In Mesoamerica, organic waste was used to cultivate gardens known as chinampas. Chinampas were highly productive, producing up to four crops a year and accounting for two-thirds of the food consumed in the city. The Aztec Empire especially valued human waste, which was collected by pepenilias (scavengers) and sold in the markets of Mexico-Tenochtitlan.

Urine was also used as a mordant in the dyeing of fabrics. During the reign of Moctezuma II, dumping waste and littering were forbidden, and the penalty could reach a sentence of death. Garbage that could not be recycled was burned, sometimes at night to illuminate public spaces.
